description: How heart rate, breathing rate, depth and lactate levels change during physical activity.
content_html:
The Body’s Immediate Response to Exercise

The moment you start exercising, your body begins a coordinated series of adjustments to match the increased energy demand of working muscles. These short-term effects happen within seconds to minutes of activity beginning — and many begin even before you start, as the body anticipates exercise. Understanding what changes, why it changes, and why it matters to a performer is the focus of this lesson.

Heart Rate Response

At rest, heart rate is typically 60–80 beats per minute (bpm). As exercise begins, heart rate rises almost immediately due to signals from the nervous system and hormones such as adrenaline. This anticipatory rise — technically called the anticipatory rise — can increase heart rate even before any physical exertion, as observed in athletes waiting on the start line.

Once exercise is underway, heart rate continues to climb in proportion to intensity. At light intensity, heart rate may stabilise at 100–120 bpm. At moderate intensity (aerobic zone), it sits between 120 and 160 bpm. At maximal intensity (all-out sprinting), heart rate can reach 180–200 bpm. The maximum heart rate is estimated by 220 minus age: a 16-year-old has a maximum of approximately 204 bpm.

The reason for the increase is straightforward: working muscles demand more oxygen. The heart compensates by beating faster, increasing the volume of blood — and therefore oxygen — delivered per minute. Cardiac output rises from roughly 5 litres per minute at rest to over 20 litres per minute during maximal exercise, driven by increases in both heart rate and stroke volume.

Key Fact

Short-term cardiovascular response: heart rate rises immediately due to nervous system signals and adrenaline; anticipatory rise occurs before exercise starts; during exercise, HR increases with intensity; both HR and stroke volume increase, raising cardiac output from ~5 L/min at rest to over 20 L/min at maximal exercise.

Breathing Rate and Depth

Alongside the cardiovascular response, the respiratory system rapidly increases both the rate and depth of breathing. At rest, a typical adult breathes about 12–20 times per minute with a tidal volume of around 0.5 litres. During maximal exercise, breathing rate can rise to 40–60 breaths per minute and tidal volume can reach 3 litres, increasing total air moved per minute (minute ventilation) from roughly 6 L/min at rest to over 100 L/min during maximal exercise.

The increased rate and depth of breathing serves two purposes: it brings more oxygen to the alveoli for gas exchange, and it removes the increased carbon dioxide produced by working muscles. CO&sub2; is a key stimulus for breathing: receptors in the brain and blood vessels detect rising CO&sub2; levels and signal the respiratory centre in the brainstem to increase the rate and depth of breathing automatically.

Both changes (rate and depth) are important. Increasing rate alone would result in shallow breathing with lots of air moving in the trachea and bronchi — the “dead space” that never reaches the alveoli. Increasing depth ensures that each breath reaches the alveoli where gas exchange can actually occur. In well-trained athletes, the body preferentially increases depth rather than rate up to moderate intensities, making breathing more efficient.

Lactate Accumulation

During low to moderate exercise, lactic acid is produced in small amounts and is cleared by the aerobic system as fast as it is made. As intensity increases past the lactate threshold, production exceeds removal and lactic acid begins to accumulate in the muscle and blood. This accumulation has several consequences for the performer: muscles begin to feel heavy and painful; coordination can deteriorate; and the performer must reduce intensity or stop.

For a GCSE performer, understanding lactate accumulation is directly relevant to race strategy and training. A 400 m runner who goes out too fast will exceed their lactate threshold early, accumulating lactic acid that impairs their ability to maintain speed in the final straight. A well-trained distance runner has a higher lactate threshold, meaning they can run faster before lactic acid begins to accumulate — one of the key benefits of regular aerobic training.

Muscle fatigue during intense exercise is partly caused by lactic acid accumulation and partly by the depletion of energy stores (particularly glycogen). After exercise ends, breathing rate remains elevated for a period — this is the excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC), sometimes called oxygen debt. During this recovery phase, oxygen is used to break down lactic acid, restore muscle glycogen, replenish the oxygen stores in haemoglobin and myoglobin, and return body temperature and heart rate to resting values.

Key Fact

Three key short-term effects: (1) Heart rate and cardiac output increase — to deliver more oxygen to working muscles. (2) Breathing rate and depth increase — to supply more oxygen to alveoli and remove more CO&sub2;. (3) Lactate accumulates if intensity exceeds the lactate threshold — causing muscle fatigue and a limit on sustained high-intensity effort.

Heart rate is not the only cardiovascular adjustment during exercise. Stroke volume also increases. As muscles contract during exercise, they squeeze the veins running through them (the “muscle pump”), propelling blood back to the heart faster. This increased venous return stretches the ventricles and causes them to contract more forcefully (Starling’s law of the heart), ejecting more blood per beat. At rest, stroke volume is around 70 ml; during exercise, it can rise to 110–130 ml in a trained person. The combined effect of increased HR and increased SV dramatically multiplies cardiac output and oxygen delivery.

Data questions often present a graph or table of heart rate, stroke volume or cardiac output at rest and during exercise. To score full marks on an interpret data question, you need to: (1) quote a specific figure from the data with units (e.g. “heart rate rose from 72 bpm to 168 bpm”); (2) identify the trend (rising, plateauing, falling); and (3) link the trend to a physiological reason or sporting implication (e.g. “the rise in HR increases cardiac output, ensuring more oxygen reaches the working leg muscles during the running phase”). Students who only quote a figure without explaining its significance, or who explain the physiology without quoting data, typically score half marks.
exam_tip_html: On data interpretation questions about heart rate or cardiac output, the mark scheme expects three elements: a figure quoted from the data with units, a trend statement, and a physiological explanation. Missing any one of these costs marks. On Explain questions about short-term effects, use the chain ‘what changes → why → consequence for performance.’ For lactate accumulation: ‘lactic acid accumulates (what) because intensity exceeds the lactate threshold and anaerobic respiration rate outpaces removal (why), causing muscle fatigue and forcing the performer to slow down (consequence).’ On Calculate questions, always show the formula (Q = SV × HR), substitute the values, and give units (ml/min or L/min).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Short-term cardiovascular responses to exercise: heart rate and stroke volume both increase, raising cardiac output from ~5 L/min at rest to 20+ L/min; anticipatory rise occurs before exercise begins due to adrenaline and nervous system signals.
  • Short-term respiratory responses: breathing rate rises (12–20 to 40–60 breaths/min) and tidal volume increases (~0.5 to ~3 L), increasing minute ventilation to supply more O&sub2; and remove more CO&sub2;.
  • Lactate accumulates when exercise intensity exceeds the lactate threshold; this causes muscle fatigue. EPOC (oxygen debt) after exercise clears lactic acid and restores the body to its resting state.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the correct definition of the anticipatory rise?
A) The rise in cardiac output that occurs during maximal exercise
B) The rise in heart rate that occurs before exercise begins in response to anticipated effort
C) The increase in stroke volume during exercise due to greater venous return
D) The rise in lactic acid before the lactate threshold is reached
practice_questions.marks: B) The rise in heart rate that occurs before exercise begins in response to anticipated effort [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A 15-year-old athlete has a heart rate of 88 bpm and a stroke volume of 82 ml at the start of exercise. Calculate her cardiac output at this point.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct working: Q = 88 × 82. 1 mark for correct answer with units: 7,216 ml/min (accept 7.216 L/min). Units required.

practice_questions.text:
The table below shows heart rate and stroke volume data for a club-level athlete at rest and during a 20-minute interval training session.

Phase            | Heart rate (bpm) | Stroke volume (ml)
Rest             | 58               | 80
Warm-up (5 min)  | 115              | 95
Interval 1       | 182              | 120
Recovery         | 130              | 98
Interval 2       | 178              | 118

Calculate the cardiac output during Interval 1 and compare it to resting cardiac output.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for Interval 1: 182 × 120 = 21,840 ml/min. 1 mark for comparison: resting Q = 58 × 80 = 4,640 ml/min; cardiac output during interval 1 is approximately 4.7 times greater, an increase of about 17,200 ml/min. Both calculations must include units. Accept correct arithmetic.

practice_questions.text: Explain the short-term effects of exercise on breathing rate and depth, and why both changes are necessary for performance.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for rate increase: breathing rate rises (from ~15 to up to 60 breaths/min) in response to rising CO2 detected by chemoreceptors, signalling the respiratory centre to increase breathing frequency. 1 mark for depth increase: tidal volume increases (~0.5 L to ~3 L) as diaphragm and intercostals contract more forcefully. 1 mark for why both are needed: increasing rate alone results in shallow breathing that doesn't fully reach the alveoli; increasing depth ensures more air enters the alveoli where gas exchange actually occurs, maximising oxygen uptake.

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens to lactic acid during high-intensity exercise and explain how this affects a performer during a 400 m race.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for description: lactic acid accumulates when exercise intensity exceeds the lactate threshold — anaerobic respiration rate outpaces the body's ability to remove lactic acid. 1 mark for physiological effect: lactic acid build-up in the muscles interferes with muscle contractions, causing the burning sensation and heavy-legged fatigue. 1 mark for performance effect: the 400 m runner must reduce speed or risks a dramatic decline in performance, particularly in the final 100 m when glycogen stores deplete and lactic acid peaks.

practice_questions.text: A university sports scientist is studying the short-term effects of exercise on two groups: trained endurance athletes and untrained individuals. She measures heart rate, stroke volume and lactate at rest and during a standardised 15-minute run at the same absolute speed. Assess the likely differences between the two groups and explain what these differences tell us about the value of aerobic training.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Predicts lower resting and exercise HR in trained athletes (bradycardia + higher SV means same cardiac output at lower HR). Trained athletes have higher stroke volume, meaning they can deliver the same cardiac output with fewer beats. Trained athletes have a higher lactate threshold, so accumulate less lactic acid at the same absolute speed, meaning they work at a lower relative intensity. Reaches a supported judgement: 'These differences demonstrate that aerobic training improves the efficiency of the cardiovascular system and extends the range within which the body can sustain aerobic energy production — both of which directly improve endurance performance.' Consistent data-referenced or sport-referenced application.
Secure (3-4): Correct comparisons on at least two measures. Partial explanation of training value.
Developing (2): One correct comparison without clear training explanation.
Emerging (1): Basic point about trained vs untrained hearts.

knowledge_checks.q: What is the 'anticipatory rise' in the context of exercise physiology?
options: An increase in cardiac output during maximal effort
A rise in heart rate before exercise begins
An increase in tidal volume during inhalation
A drop in lactic acid after warm-up

knowledge_checks.q: What causes the accumulation of lactic acid during intense exercise?
options: Aerobic respiration producing too much CO2
Anaerobic respiration producing lactic acid faster than it is removed
A drop in heart rate below the aerobic threshold

knowledge_checks.q: Minute ventilation is calculated as tidal volume multiplied by _____ rate.
Match each short-term effect to its cause during exercise:
right: Nervous system + adrenaline signal heart to beat faster
Diaphragm and intercostals contract more forcefully

flashcard_questions.q: What is the anticipatory rise in heart rate?
flashcard_questions.a: Heart rate rises before exercise starts in response to anticipated effort.

flashcard_questions.q: How does cardiac output change during maximal exercise?
flashcard_questions.a: Rises from ~5 L/min at rest to over 20 L/min, due to increases in both HR and SV.
Tidal volume multiplied by breathing rate — total air moved per minute.

flashcard_questions.q: How does breathing rate change from rest to maximal exercise?
flashcard_questions.a: Rises from ~15 to up to 60 breaths per minute.

flashcard_questions.q: What stimulus causes breathing rate to increase during exercise?
flashcard_questions.a: Rising CO2 detected by chemoreceptors, signalling the respiratory centre.

flashcard_questions.q: What is EPOC and what is it used for?
flashcard_questions.a: Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption — clears lactic acid and restores resting state.
The intensity at which lactic acid accumulates faster than it can be removed.

flashcard_questions.q: How does stroke volume change during exercise?
flashcard_questions.a: Increases from ~70 ml at rest to 110-130 ml due to greater venous return.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the estimated maximum heart rate for a 16-year-old?
Why does lactic acid cause muscle fatigue?
flashcard_questions.a: It interferes with muscle contractions, causing pain and reducing performance.

glossary_terms.definition: The rise in heart rate that occurs before exercise begins, in response to the body anticipating physical effort.
The highest heart rate an individual can safely reach during maximal exercise, estimated as 220 minus the person's age.
The volume of blood ejected by the heart per minute, equal to stroke volume multiplied by heart rate.
The total volume of air breathed in one minute, calculated as tidal volume multiplied by breathing rate.
The exercise intensity at which lactic acid production exceeds the rate at which it can be removed, leading to accumulation in the blood and muscles.
The burning sensation and heavy-legged feeling experienced during high-intensity exercise due to the accumulation of lactic acid and related metabolic changes.
Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption — the elevated rate of oxygen consumption after exercise that helps remove lactic acid, restore oxygen stores and return the body to its resting state.
The volume of blood ejected from the left ventricle with each heartbeat, which increases during exercise as venous return to the heart rises.
